title: Forces and Motion
bigQuestion: How can we predict what a push or a pull will do to an object?

story.title: The Rope That Would Not Move
story.kicker: Twenty kids pulled as hard as they could, and the flag in the middle stayed right where it was.
paragraphs: It was field day at a school on Chicago's South Side. Two teams of ten grabbed a thick rope. A red flag was tied to the middle. A chalk line on the grass marked the center. The teacher yelled, "Pull!" Everyone leaned back. Faces turned red. Shoes dug into the dirt. And the flag did not move. Not one inch.

This seemed strange. Twenty kids were pulling with all their strength. The rope was stretched tight. Yet nothing changed. If you looked only at the flag, you might think nobody was pulling at all. But the kids' shaking arms told a different story. Something big was happening. It just was not motion.

Then one girl on the left team slipped. Her foot skidded on a patch of mud. For one second her pull was gone. Right away the flag jumped toward the right team. The whole left team stumbled forward. The right team fell in a heap, laughing. The chalk line was far behind the flag now.

That one slip tells you almost everything about forces. Two pulls that match each other cancel out. The rope goes nowhere. But make one pull a little stronger, and motion starts at once. Scientists have a name for each case. This chapter is about those names and the patterns behind them.
story.think: The flag did not move at first. Does that mean no force was acting on it? What is your evidence?

lessons.title: What a Force Is
lessons.mainIdea: A force is a push or a pull, and every force has a strength and a direction.
reading: Kick a soccer ball and it rolls away. Pull a wagon and it follows you. Both of these are examples of a *force*. A force is simply a push or a pull. You cannot see a force itself. You can only see what it does to an object. When you watch something start, stop, speed up, or turn, a force is at work.

Every force has two parts. The first is *strength*. A gentle tap on a ball is a weak force. A hard kick is a strong force. The second part is *direction*. A push to the left and a push to the right are different forces. Scientists draw a force as an arrow. A longer arrow means a stronger push. The arrow points the way the push goes.

Try this with a door. Push it near the handle and it swings easily. Push the same door right next to the hinges and it will barely budge. Same strength, different place, different result. Where and which way you push matters as much as how hard. When we describe a force, we always name both its strength and its direction.

words.d: a push or a pull on an object
how hard a force pushes or pulls
the way a force pushes or pulls, such as left, right, up or down

look.title: Arrows on a Shopping Cart
look.text: Picture a shopping cart in a parking lot. A child pushes it gently from behind. At the same time, the wind pushes it from the side. Draw the cart from above. Draw one arrow for the child's push and one for the wind. Make the child's arrow longer, because that push is stronger.
look.prompt: Which way do you think the cart will roll? Why not straight ahead?

check.q: What is a force?
choices: A kind of energy stored in food
check.why: A force is a push or a pull. You see it by what it does to an object.

check.q: Two students push a box with the same strength but in different directions. What is different about their forces?
choices: Nothing; the forces are the same
check.why: Every force has a strength and a direction. Here the strengths match, so the direction is what differs.

check.q: Why does a door open easily near the handle but not near the hinges?
choices: The push near the handle is stronger
The push near the hinges is in the wrong place to turn the door
check.why: The strength was the same. Where and which way you push changes what the force does.

lessons.title: Balanced Forces
lessons.mainIdea: When forces on an object are balanced, they cancel out and the object's motion does not change.
reading: Think back to the tug-of-war. Both teams pulled hard, but the flag stayed still. The two pulls were equal in strength and opposite in direction. We call forces like this *balanced*. Balanced forces *cancel* each other out. It is as if no force were acting at all. The flag did not move because there was no leftover pull in any direction.

Balanced forces are everywhere. A book sits on a table. Gravity pulls the book down. The table pushes the book up with exactly the same strength. The book stays put. You sit in a chair right now. The chair pushes up as hard as your weight pushes down. If it did not, you would sink through it.

Here is a surprise. Balanced forces do not only keep things still. They also keep moving things moving at a steady speed. A hockey puck sliding on very smooth ice keeps going in a straight line. No force is winning. The puck's motion does not change. Balanced forces mean no change, whether the object is resting or moving.

words.d: forces that are equal in strength and opposite in direction
to undo each other so the total effect is zero

look.title: Newton's First Law
look.text: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a right line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed thereon.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia, 1687, in Andrew Motte's English translation of 1729
look.prompt: Put Newton's sentence in your own words. What does 'perseveres in its state of rest' mean for the flag in the tug-of-war?

check.q: Which situation shows balanced forces?
choices: A book resting on a table
A ball rolling faster down a hill
A bike slowing to a stop
check.why: Gravity pulls the book down and the table pushes it up just as hard. Its motion does not change.

check.q: A puck slides across smooth ice at a steady speed in a straight line. What is true about the forces on it?
choices: A strong force keeps pushing it forward
The forces are balanced, so its motion does not change
No forces at all touch the puck
check.why: Gravity and the ice's push cancel. With balanced forces, steady motion stays steady.

check.q: Why does a table hold a book up instead of letting it fall?
choices: Gravity stops working on the table
The table pushes up on the book as hard as gravity pulls down
The book is too light for gravity
check.why: The table's upward push balances gravity's downward pull, so the book stays still.

lessons.title: Unbalanced Forces Change Motion
lessons.mainIdea: An unbalanced force makes an object speed up, slow down, or change direction.
reading: When the girl in the tug-of-war slipped, the pulls stopped matching. The right team's pull was now stronger. The forces were *unbalanced*. The rope moved toward the stronger pull right away. Any time forces do not cancel, motion changes. This is the rule that lets you predict what happens next.

An unbalanced force can change motion in three ways. It can make an object start or speed up. Think of a kick on a still ball. It can make an object slow down or stop. Think of a catcher's mitt on a pitch. Or it can change direction, like a bat sending a pitch into the air. In each case, look for the force that is not being canceled.

The size of the change depends on two things. A stronger force makes a bigger change. A heavier object changes less for the same force. Push a shopping cart that is empty and it zips away. Push a full one with the same strength and it barely moves. Scientists call the amount of stuff in an object its *mass*. More mass means harder to change.

words.d: forces that do not cancel, so one direction wins
the amount of matter in an object; more mass makes it harder to speed up or slow down

look.title: The Slip
look.text: Imagine watching the tug-of-war in slow motion. Before the slip, the arrows on each side are the same length and point opposite ways. Then the girl's foot skids. Her arrow disappears. The left team's total arrow is now shorter than the right team's. Draw the two arrows before the slip and after.
look.prompt: After the slip, which way does the flag move? What would happen if the left team had twice as many students?

check.q: A rolling ball on the floor slows down and stops. What must be true?
choices: An unbalanced force acted against its motion
check.why: Motion changed, so the forces were unbalanced. Friction pushed against the rolling.

check.q: You push an empty cart and then a full cart with the same strength. What happens?
choices: The empty cart speeds up more because it has less mass
Both carts speed up the same amount
The full cart speeds up more because it is heavier
check.why: The same force changes the motion of a low-mass object more than a high-mass one.

check.q: Which is an example of a force changing an object's direction?
choices: A car sitting at a red light
A bat hitting a pitched baseball
A book resting on a desk
A puck sliding at a steady speed
check.why: The bat's push sends the ball a new way. The other examples show no change in motion.

lessons.title: Gravity Pulls Everything Down
lessons.mainIdea: Gravity is a pull toward the center of Earth that acts on every object, all the time.
reading: Drop a pencil and it falls to the floor. It never falls up or sideways. The force that pulls it is *gravity*. Gravity is a pull between objects that have mass. Earth has an enormous mass. So Earth pulls hard on everything near it. The pull always points toward Earth's center. That is what we mean by "down."

You feel gravity as *weight*. Your weight is the strength of Earth's pull on you. A scale measures that pull. Gravity acts even when you are not falling. Stand still, and gravity pulls you down while the floor pushes you up. Jump, and for a moment the floor stops pushing. Gravity wins, and you come back down.

Gravity does not need to touch you. It pulls across empty space. That is how Earth keeps the Moon circling around it. It is also why a ball thrown up always comes back. As the ball rises, gravity slows it. At the top it stops for an instant. Then gravity pulls it faster and faster toward the ground.

words.d: a pull between objects that have mass; Earth's gravity pulls things toward its center
the strength of gravity's pull on an object

look.title: How Hard Different Worlds Pull
look.prompt: A student weighs 60 pounds on Earth. Roughly what would a scale read on the Moon? On Jupiter?

check.q: Which way does gravity pull an object near Earth?
check.why: Gravity always pulls toward Earth's center. That direction is what we call down.

check.q: What does a bathroom scale measure?
choices: The strength of Earth's pull on you
check.why: Weight is the strength of gravity's pull on you, and that is what the scale reads.

check.q: A ball is thrown straight up. What does gravity do while the ball rises?
choices: Turns off until the ball stops
check.why: Gravity keeps pulling down the whole time, so the rising ball slows until it stops and falls.

lessons.title: Friction Slows Things Down
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is a force between surfaces that rub, and it always pushes against the motion.
reading: Slide a book across a table. It stops after a short distance. Slide it across ice and it goes much farther. The force that stopped the book is *friction*. Friction happens when two surfaces rub against each other. Even smooth-looking surfaces have tiny bumps. The bumps catch on each other and resist the motion.

Friction always pushes against the direction of motion. That makes it a great brake. Bike brakes squeeze rubber pads against the wheel. Car tires grip the road. Sandpaper grips wood. In Chicago winters, crews spread salt and sand on icy sidewalks. The grit adds friction so shoes and tires can hold on.

Sometimes we want less friction. Oil on a bike chain lets it spin freely. Wax on a sled lets it fly down the hill. A hockey rink is kept smooth so pucks glide. *Rough* surfaces make more friction. *Smooth* surfaces make less. Engineers add friction where things must grip and remove it where things must slide.

words.d: a force that slows things that rub together
bumpy or uneven; rough surfaces make more friction
flat and even; smooth surfaces make less friction

look.title: Same Push, Four Floors
look.text: A student pushes a wooden block with the same strength on four surfaces: a carpet, a wood floor, a tile floor, and a sheet of ice. On carpet the block goes 20 centimeters. On wood it goes 60. On tile it goes 90. On ice it slides across the whole room.
look.prompt: Rank the four surfaces from most friction to least. What do you think would happen with a rubber block instead of wood?

check.q: Why does a sliding book stop on a table?
choices: Friction between the book and table pushes against its motion
The book runs out of energy inside
The table pulls it toward the middle
check.why: Friction acts against the motion. It slows the book until it stops.

check.q: Why do road crews spread sand on icy sidewalks?
choices: To melt the ice with heat
To add friction so shoes can grip
check.why: Grit makes the surface rougher, and rougher surfaces have more friction.

check.q: Where would a sled slide the farthest with the same push?
check.why: Ice is the smoothest surface, so it has the least friction to slow the sled.

lessons.title: The Swing of a Pendulum
lessons.mainIdea: A pendulum swings in a repeating pattern, and that pattern lets you predict its next swing.
reading: Tie a washer to a string and let it hang. Pull it to the side and let go. It swings back and forth, back and forth. This is a *pendulum*. Gravity pulls the washer down toward the middle. It overshoots, rises on the other side, and gravity pulls it back. The swings get smaller as air friction steals a bit of motion each time.

Time the swings and you will find a *pattern*. Each full swing takes almost the same time as the one before. A short string swings quickly. A long string swings slowly. Strangely, a heavy washer and a light washer on the same string keep the same time. The length is what matters, not the weight.

Once you know the pattern, you can *predict*. If ten swings took 20 seconds, the next ten will take about 20 seconds too. Long ago, people used this pattern to build clocks. A swinging pendulum ticked off the seconds. Any time motion repeats, watch for the pattern. The pattern is what makes the future easy to guess.

words.d: a weight hanging from a string or rod that swings back and forth
something that repeats in a way you can count on
to say what will happen before it happens, using a pattern or evidence

look.title: Longer String, Slower Swing
look.prompt: What happens to the swing time when the string gets four times longer? Predict the time for a 9 m string.

check.q: Which change makes a pendulum swing more slowly?
check.why: The length of the string sets the swing time. Longer strings swing more slowly.

check.q: Ten swings of a pendulum took 15 seconds. About how long will the next ten swings take?
check.why: Each swing takes about the same time, so the pattern repeats: about 15 seconds.

check.q: What force pulls the pendulum back toward the middle on every swing?
check.why: Gravity pulls the washer down toward the lowest point every time it rises.

lessons.title: A Ball on a Ramp
lessons.mainIdea: A ball speeds up as it rolls down a ramp in a steady pattern that Galileo measured and you can measure too.
reading: Roll a ball down a *ramp*. It starts slow and gets faster and faster. Gravity pulls it down the slope the whole way. The pull is steady, so the speed keeps growing. About 400 years ago, an Italian scientist named Galileo studied this. He wanted to know exactly how falling objects speed up. Free fall was too fast to time. So he slowed it down with a ramp.

Galileo rolled bronze balls down a long, smooth groove. He timed each roll. He found a clear *pattern*. In the second stretch of time, the ball went three times as far as in the first. In the third, five times as far. The distance grew by odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7. This pattern held no matter how steep the ramp was.

You can test this yourself. Mark a ramp every 10 centimeters. Let the ball go and count out loud at a steady beat. Notice where the ball is on each count. Then make the ramp steeper and try again. A steeper ramp means a bigger pull down the slope. The ball speeds up faster. But the odd-number pattern shows up again. Patterns like this let scientists *predict* motion before it happens.

words.d: a sloped surface that an object can roll or slide along
something that repeats in a way you can count on
to say what will happen before it happens, using a pattern or evidence

look.title: Galileo's Groove
look.text: Galileo describes a wooden beam about 12 cubits long with a smooth, straight groove cut into it and lined with parchment. He rolled a hard, smooth bronze ball down the groove and timed each roll by weighing the water that dripped from a bucket while the ball moved. He repeated each roll many times, and found that the distances always grew with the square of the time.
look.cite: Galileo Galilei, Two New Sciences, 1638 (paraphrased from the 1914 English translation)
look.prompt: Why did Galileo repeat each roll many times instead of trusting one measurement?

check.q: Why did Galileo use a ramp instead of dropping balls straight down?
choices: He did not own a tall tower
A ramp slows the motion enough to time it
check.why: Free fall was too fast for his clocks. A gentle slope made the same kind of motion slow enough to measure.

check.q: A ball rolls down a ramp. What happens to its speed as it goes?
check.why: Gravity keeps pulling the ball down the slope, so it keeps speeding up.

check.q: If a ball travels 1 unit in the first count and 3 units in the second, how far will it travel in the third count if the pattern holds?
check.why: Galileo's pattern grows by odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7. The third stretch is 5 units.

lessons.title: Magnets Push and Pull
lessons.mainIdea: A magnet can push or pull certain objects without touching them, and its two poles behave differently.
reading: Hold a magnet near a paper clip. The clip jumps across the gap and sticks. Nothing touched the clip until it moved. The pull came from the *magnet* itself. Magnets attract some metals, mostly iron and steel. They ignore copper, aluminum, wood, and plastic. Test this around you. A steel refrigerator door will hold a magnet, but an aluminum soda can will not.

Every magnet has two ends called *poles*, north and south. Bring two north poles together and they push apart. You can feel the push in your fingers. Turn one magnet around and the north and south poles snap together. Opposite poles *attract*. Like poles *repel*. The push and pull get stronger as the magnets get closer.

Earth itself acts like a giant magnet. That is why a compass needle turns to point north. Sailors used compasses for hundreds of years before anyone knew why they worked. In the year 1600, an English doctor named William Gilbert tested lodestones, which are natural magnets. He argued that the whole Earth was one great magnet. His evidence was the compass.

words.d: an object that pulls on iron and steel and can push or pull other magnets
the two ends of a magnet, called north and south
to pull toward
to push away

look.title: Gilbert's Little Earth
look.text: In his 1600 book on magnets, William Gilbert described shaping a lodestone into a ball he called a terrella, or 'little Earth.' When he moved a small compass needle around the ball, the needle turned the way compass needles do on the real Earth. From this he argued that Earth itself is a great magnet.
look.prompt: What did Gilbert observe, and what idea did he build from that observation?

check.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
check.why: Magnets attract iron and steel. Copper, plastic, and wood are not attracted.

check.q: You bring the north pole of one magnet near the north pole of another. What happens?
check.why: Like poles repel. Two north poles push away from each other.

check.q: Why does a compass needle point north?
choices: Earth acts like a giant magnet
The needle is heavier on one end
check.why: The needle is a small magnet, and Earth's magnetism turns it toward the north.

lessons.title: Static Electricity
lessons.mainIdea: Rubbing some materials together builds up static electricity, which can push or pull objects without touching them.
reading: Rub a balloon on your hair. Hold it near a wall and it sticks. Hold it near tiny bits of paper and they leap up. Your hair may even stand on end. This is *static electricity*. Rubbing moves tiny bits of electric *charge* from one object to the other. The balloon ends up with extra charge. The extra charge pulls on the paper from a distance.

There are two kinds of charge, called positive and negative. Like charges push apart. Opposite charges pull together. That sounds a lot like magnets. But charge and magnetism are not the same thing. A charged balloon does not pick up a paper clip. A magnet does not attract paper bits. Each one has its own kind of force.

In a dry Chicago winter, static shows up everywhere. Pull off a wool hat and your hair crackles. Touch a doorknob and you feel a tiny zap. The zap is a little spark. Charge that built up on you jumps to the metal. Lightning is the same thing on a giant scale. Charge builds in a storm cloud and then jumps in one huge spark.

words.d: extra electric charge that builds up on an object, often from rubbing
a property of tiny particles that makes them push or pull on each other; it comes in positive and negative

look.title: Sparks From a Key
look.text: In a 1752 letter, Benjamin Franklin described flying a kite with a pointed wire during a thunderstorm. A metal key hung from the kite string. Once the string grew wet, he wrote, sparks could be drawn from the key with a knuckle, just like the sparks from a rubbed glass tube. This was his evidence that lightning was electric.
look.cite: Benjamin Franklin, letter to Peter Collinson, 1752 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What did Franklin compare the spark from the key to? Why did that comparison matter?

check.q: What happens when you rub a balloon on your hair?
choices: Charge moves between the hair and the balloon
check.why: Rubbing moves charge from one object to the other. That extra charge is static electricity.

check.q: Two objects both carry negative charge. What will they do?
check.why: Like charges repel, so two negative objects push away from each other.

check.q: What is the tiny zap you feel when touching a doorknob?
choices: A small spark of charge jumping to the metal
check.why: Charge that built up on you jumps to the metal knob as a tiny spark.

lessons.title: Solving a Problem With Magnets
lessons.mainIdea: Engineers use pushes and pulls, like the pull of a magnet, to design solutions to everyday problems.
reading: A cabinet door in a classroom keeps swinging open. Books fall out. The class decides to fix it. They need something that holds the door shut but lets it open with a small pull. A magnet is perfect. A small magnet on the frame and a steel plate on the door make a *latch*. The magnet's pull holds the door. A tug stronger than that pull opens it.

This is *engineering*: using science to solve a problem. First the class defines the problem clearly. The door must stay shut on its own but open easily. Then they test ideas. One magnet is too weak; the door drifts open. Three magnets are too strong; small hands cannot open it. Two magnets are just right. Testing tells them which design works.

Magnets solve many problems this way. Refrigerator doors seal with a magnetic strip. Some phone chargers snap on with magnets. Cranes in scrap yards lift whole cars with huge electromagnets. Some trains float above their tracks on magnetic pushes. Every one of these designs started with a problem and a test.

words.d: a device that holds a door or lid closed
using science and testing to design a solution to a problem

look.title: Design a Better Latch
look.text: Your class has three magnets of different strengths, a steel plate, tape, and a cabinet door that keeps swinging open. A first-grade class will use the cabinet. Their hands are small and not very strong. You need the door to stay closed when the room is bumped, but open with one finger.
look.prompt: Which magnet would you try first, and how would you test whether it is too strong or too weak?

check.q: What holds a magnetic latch closed?
choices: The pull between the magnet and the steel plate
Friction between the door and frame
check.why: The magnet attracts the steel plate. That pull keeps the door shut until a stronger tug opens it.

check.q: The class found one magnet was too weak and three were too strong. What did they learn from testing?
choices: Magnets do not work on doors
Two magnets would likely be the right strength
The door needs a lock instead
check.why: Testing showed the right strength was between one and three magnets.

check.q: What is the first step in solving an engineering problem?
choices: Define clearly what the solution must do
check.why: A clear problem tells you what to test for. Then you can tell if a design works.

review.q: In the tug-of-war story, why did the flag stay still at first?
choices: The two teams' pulls were balanced
review.why: Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out, so the flag's motion did not change.

review.q: What two things describe every force?
review.why: A force is drawn as an arrow: its length is the strength and it points in the direction.

review.q: A soccer ball rolls across grass and slows to a stop. Which force slows it?
review.why: Friction between the ball and the grass pushes against the motion.

review.q: Which of these shows an unbalanced force at work?
choices: A lamp sitting on a desk
A puck gliding at a steady speed
A sled speeding up down a hill
review.why: Speeding up is a change in motion, and only unbalanced forces change motion.

review.q: A pendulum with a 1 m string takes 2 seconds per swing. Which pendulum would take longer?
review.why: Longer strings swing more slowly. The weight of the washer does not change the time.

choices: A north pole and a south pole
A magnet and a paper clip
A magnet and a steel door
review.why: Like poles repel. Opposite poles and magnets near steel attract.

review.q: What did Galileo's ramp experiments show about a rolling ball?
choices: It moves at a constant speed
It slows down as it rolls
It speeds up in a regular pattern
review.why: The distances grew by odd numbers, 1, 3, 5, 7, showing a steady speeding up.

review.q: A charged balloon sticks to a wall. What makes it stick?
choices: Static electricity pulling from a distance
review.why: The extra charge on the balloon pulls on the wall without touching it.
